rationale: The canonical, model-agnostic feature-attribution method -- explicitly designed to generalise across model types via a consistent game-theoretic formulation -- directly answers RQ21's question of how mechanistic analysis can improve understanding of model behaviour and how generalisable such methods are across models.

Directly matches RQ21's own phrasing -- 'mechanistic analysis of model internals, such as weights, activations' -- as a tool purpose-built to inspect and manipulate exactly those internals, complementing repe/vgel-repeng's representation-engineering-specific approach with a general interpretability/intervention API.

Meta's official PyTorch interpretability library requires full (white-box) access to compute its attributions -- exactly RQ54's access-level framing -- and its methods are usable to check claimed model properties, alongside ai-explainability-360's model-agnostic approach.

Purpose-built to systematically scan a model/agent for weaknesses and vulnerabilities before deployment -- a meta-evaluation tool aimed squarely at surfacing blindspots -- which is a more precise fit for RQ19's question than a general eval-running framework.
Microsoft's own official framework for scaling and automating red-teaming of generative AI systems is a direct, high-credibility answer to RQ22, complementing garak/project-moonshot/argus-redteam.

Federated learning is a distinct, major privacy-enhancing technique for reconciling data access with privacy-preserving ML -- RQ30's question -- not yet represented in the catalog alongside differential privacy, MPC, homomorphic encryption and synthetic data; Flower is the leading standalone open-source FL framework.

PySyft's entire design is remote, audited computation over data that never leaves its owner's server -- a direct, general-purpose implementation of structuring third-party data access to preserve privacy while enabling meaningful analysis/auditing, RQ29's exact question.

A standardized, widely-cited benchmark for measuring adversarial robustness gives a concrete way to track whether detection/defense methods are actually improving over time -- RQ86's question -- complementing open-prompt-injection's LLM-prompt-injection-specific angle with the classical vision/classifier adversarial-robustness space.

Implements policy-based blocking of specific dangerous action types (e.g. an agent permitted to query a database must not be permitted to drop a table) at the point of invocation, a concrete gating mechanism for dual-use capability requests -- RQ89's question -- complementing nemo-guardrails' prompt-level gating with agent-action-level gating.

One of the most widely cited standards for what 'safety and reliability' concretely means for an LLM application, operationalized as ten named risk categories -- a citable standard rather than a software suite, distinct in kind from the assessment tools already mapped here (aisev/compl-ai/decodingtrust/trustllm/infosys-responsible-ai-toolkit/project-moonshot).

Meta's official watermarking implementation extends metadata watermarking to the video modality specifically -- markllm and c2pa-rs cover text/general provenance, but neither is video-native -- directly answering RQ66's question of how metadata watermarking can be applied to AI-generated content.

Unlike a bare manifest standard, Machine Genome is both a protocol *and* a live registry (machinegenome.org, HTTP API) recording cryptographically-signed lineage across models/agents/datasets -- a genuine audit registry providing end-to-end verification along the value chain, RQ59's exact question.

Purpose-built to quantitatively evaluate data attribution methods themselves (not just perform attribution), directly answering RQ12's question of whether behaviours can be accurately attributed to training data, as a meta-evaluation complement to llm-attributor's implement role.

Assurance cases are the safety-engineering community's established methodology (used in aviation/nuclear safety cases) for standardising what counts as adequate justification of a safety/reliability claim despite incomplete understanding of the underlying system -- directly RQ92's question -- a structured-argumentation approach distinct in kind from the assessment-suite tools already mapped here.

Runs multiple membership-inference attack methods (LiRA, QMIA, structural attacks) at scale to produce a per-record vulnerability report, directly answering RQ46's question of optimising membership inference for large-scale training-data verification, complementing ml-privacy-meter with a second implementation plus an ante-hoc (pre-training) risk-assessment mode ml-privacy-meter lacks.

A genuine queryable provenance registry (not just a manifest format) -- capturing and persistently storing workflow/task/artifact lineage with a REST API for later querying -- directly implements the audit-registry capability RQ59 asks about, backed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

A mature, competition-ranked formal verification tool that requires full model access to prove or disprove specified properties on real deep-network architectures -- a much stronger and more general answer to RQ54 than a bare explanation method, distinct from the earlier-rejected leanverifier (pre-release, affine-classifiers-only) precisely by being production-grade and architecture-general.

The long-standing open-source standard for volunteer/grid computing, with a scheduler that allocates shared compute across projects via resource-share weighting and credit accounting -- a direct, mature, working answer to RQ33's question of how public compute resources can be allocated fairly and equitably between users. Surfaced by mining an awesome-list this session had already logged as a link-list reject; not found by ~90+ free-text keyword angles or 25 topic-tag sweeps.

MLflow's Model Registry is arguably the most widely-adopted open-source model registry, directly implementing versioned tracking of model updates -- RQ56's question. Note: mlflow/mlflow was previously rejected in this project's rgaf-seed-triage round, but that judgment was specifically about MemAlign, a narrow feature bundled inside MLflow, not MLflow's own core registry capability, which was never separately evaluated until now.

OPA's own core framing -- 'can user X call operation Y on resource Z' -- is a literal, industry-standard implementation of authorising a verified user identity as a gate for invoking a specific capability, directly answering RQ90 and resolving it from zero coverage.

An EU-funded (FAIRsFAIR project), actively-maintained service that automatically audits a dataset against the FAIR principles and produces a score is direct infrastructure for enabling researchers to audit large datasets -- RQ8's question -- complementing croissant/frictionless-data-package's metadata-description role with an actual assessment/scoring role.

Operationalizes EU AI Act risk classification into a scored assessment -- a second, jurisdiction-distinct instance of RQ91's question about which system properties can serve as reliable risk/regulatory indicators, alongside Canada's aia-eia-js. Correction: this repo was previously logged via a bulk rule-based reject pass (generic 'low-substance' fallback) without individual review; on individual review it is a legitimate, active, focused tool.

A centralized, hostable rule/skill layer that AI coding assistants consult before and during generation to gate output against specific safety requirements (secure coding practices) is a concrete instance of RQ55's question -- assessing risk in a given context/query/response for compliance with safety requirements -- specialised to the code-generation context, distinct from the general-purpose LLM guardrails (guardrailsai/nemo-guardrails) already mapped here.

Systematically maps AI-lifecycle components to specific risks and controls (not just a flat risk list) as machine-readable data plus an interactive explorer, a direct, cross-industry-backed answer to RQ91's question of which system properties can serve as reliable risk indicators and regulatory targets.

Confident learning is explicitly designed to scale problematic-data identification (label errors, outliers, near-duplicates) to large real-world datasets -- a direct, near-verbatim answer to RQ1's question, and a very well-established tool (11.6k stars) that was a surprising gap in the catalog.

Google's official library for computing macro-scale dataset statistics and detecting distributional anomalies/skew is a direct answer to RQ9's question of how macro-scale dataset properties such as persistent bias can be identified and measured, complementing the existing model-output-focused fairness metrics with a dataset-statistics-focused approach.

A comprehensive suite of automated checks specifically designed to catch evaluation blindspots (data leakage, drift, weak spots) is a direct working answer to RQ19's question of measuring evaluation thoroughness and identifying blindspots, complementing giskard's LLM/agent-specific scanning with broader model+data validation coverage.

Automatically extracts and reports exactly the licence and metadata fields RQ7 asks about -- generating a standards-compliant (CycloneDX) machine-readable record with a completeness score that flags what's missing -- a production OWASP GenAI Security Project tool, not a proposal.

A versioned, CI-tested (v0.3.0) OWASP scanner purpose-built to audit GenAI applications' data pipelines against a 21-control risk taxonomy -- direct infrastructure for enabling researchers/practitioners to audit large datasets and their handling, RQ8's question.

Cross-references an AI system against multiple integrated risk taxonomies (including the MIT AI Risk Repository, this project's own cited taxonomy source) to surface applicable risks and map them to mitigations -- a working, programmatic answer to RQ91's question of which system properties indicate risk, via a knowledge-graph mechanism distinct from aia-eia-js/euconform's questionnaire-scoring approach and cosai-risk-map's flat component-risk-control mapping.

A W3C-standardised, machine-readable vocabulary specifically for describing data-handling and privacy properties (purpose, legal basis, categories, measures) is a direct, standards-body answer to RQ7's question of what licence and metadata reporting requirements assist responsible data practices, complementing spdx3/frai's licence-and-compliance-evidence focus with a privacy-specific vocabulary.

Defines schema fields specifically for a dataset's labeling/annotation provenance (who labeled it, with what tool, under what process) -- information croissant/frictionless-data-package don't specifically schematise -- directly answering RQ10's question of what information is necessary for determining a dataset's suitability for training. Low adoption (7 stars) noted honestly; included for the schema's direct textual fit, not credibility.

Requires genuine white-box access to a model's weights, tokenizer and architecture metadata to detect derivation from a known base model -- a direct demonstration of how full model access (as opposed to output-only black-box access) enables detecting theft/duplication, RQ38's question. A stronger fit than the earlier-removed embedding-fingerprints mapping, which only needed output-embedding access and didn't engage the access-continuum framing.

Fast, highly accurate content-type detection independent of file extension is directly usable to scale identification of mislabeled, disguised, or unexpected file types within massive training corpora -- RQ1's question -- via a distinct mechanism (content classification) from the existing PII/label-error-focused tools at RQ1.
